# Draft:Thirumakkottai Arulmigu Gnanapureeswarar Swamy Temple

----
The Thirumakkottai Arulmigu Gnanapureeswarar Temple is a Hindu temple located in the Mannargudi taluk of Thanjavur district in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu. The temple is associated with the Chola period and is believed to have a history of over 1000 years, supported by multiple inscriptions found within the temple परिसर.
Names
The temple has been referred to by several names in historical and traditional sources, including Gnanapureesuram, Pachima Parijatha Vanam, Thirumeignaanapuram, Thirumelkottai, and Thirumakkottai.
History and inscriptions
The temple contains a number of stone inscriptions and copper plate records that indicate its antiquity and historical significance. A total of twelve stone inscriptions and two copper plate inscriptions have been identified within the temple.
Inscriptions from the Chola period include those attributed to the reigns of Rajaraja Chola I (r. 985–1014 CE), Kulothunga Chola I, and Rajaraja Chola III. Inscriptions from the Pandya period, particularly from the time of Maravarman Kulasekara Pandyan, are also present.
During the Vijayanagara period, the temple is believed to have undergone renovation works under the reign of Achyuta Deva Maharaya (r. 1529–1542 CE).
One of the earliest inscriptions in the temple is dated to approximately 998 CE, during the reign of Rajaraja Chola I. Additional inscriptions include four from Rajaraja Chola III, two from Kulasekara Pandyan, one from Achyuta Deva Maharaya, and three inscriptions without clearly identified rulers.
Copper plate inscriptions associated with the temple are attributed to the Thanjavur Maratha period, with references to the reign of Serfoji (Sarabhoji) and dating to around the 16th century CE.
Religious and traditional significance
According to temple tradition, the site is associated with various religious legends. It is identified as Pachima Parijatha Vanam, as it is located to the west of Thirukkalar, which is traditionally referred to as Parijatha Vanam.
Temple traditions describe that a group of sages sought spiritual knowledge and were guided to attain it through the chanting of the Panchakshara mantra ("Namashivaya"). Sage Vasishta is believed to have performed penance at this site and consecrated a Shiva Lingam, leading to the association of the presiding deity with the name Gnanapureeswarar.
The temple is also traditionally linked to the Ramayana, where it is believed that Lord Rama visited the site and received spiritual instruction from Sage Vasishta.
Temple tank
The temple tank located in front of the temple is known as Gnana Theertham or Perunoi Piritha Theertham. According to local tradition, the tank is associated with healing and spiritual significance.
Architecture
The temple complex measures approximately 283 feet in length and 211 feet in width and consists of three concentric enclosures (prakaras).
The presiding deity is Lord Gnanapureeswarar, represented as a self-manifested (swayambhu) Shiva Lingam. The consort deity is Goddess Periyanayaki (Brihannayaki), whose shrine faces south.
A notable feature of the temple is the presence of sixteen forms of Ganesha, leading to its identification as a Sodasa Ganapathi sthalam. Another distinctive feature is the absence of traditional Dwarapalakas, with Ganesha and Murugan depicted as guardians at the entrance.
Other shrines within the temple complex include those dedicated to Vasishta Rishi, Dakshinamurthy, Somaskandar, Vishwanathar, Pragatheeswarar, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Murugan with consorts Valli and Deivanai, Navagrahas, Bhairava, and Surya.
Inscriptions and copper plates
The copper plate inscriptions associated with the temple provide details of land grants, donations, and administrative arrangements. These records mention contributions from local chieftains, administrators, and agricultural communities, indicating the temple’s role in the socio-economic structure of the region.
The inscriptions also refer to charitable endowments (dharma) made for temple rituals and maintenance. Some records include stipulations regarding the proper execution of these endowments and describe religious merit associated with their fulfillment.
Administration
The temple owns agricultural lands spanning over 900 acres across multiple villages in the region. Since 1945, the temple has been administered under the control of the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments (H.R. & C.E.) Department of Tamil Nadu, managed by an Executive Officer and trustees.
Religious classification
The temple is considered a Devara Vaippu Sthalam, referring to shrines mentioned in the hymns of the Tamil Saivite saints (Nayanmars) without having dedicated hymns.
Sacred tree
The sacred tree (sthala vriksha) of the temple is the Parijatha tree (Nyctanthes arbor-tristis).
